new_statements.quote: Estos son los únicos signos modales. Para la acentuación pinto el acento allí donde lo he oído de viva voz, pues por regla general puede asentarse que el acento carga sobre la última sílaba.
new_statements.translation: These are the only modal signs. For accentuation I write the accent where I have heard it spoken aloud, since as a general rule it can be stated that the accent falls on the last syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Verification done from the copies we hold under (1) Quote: I re-rendered PDF pages 309-317 of 526 pp., no text) into the and read the page scan. PDF page 309 is the title page 'Gramática y vocabulario de la lengua que hablan los indios Darienes.. obra escrita por el señor doctor don José Vicente Uribe.. copiada de los manuscritos originales, y bajo la inspección del autor, por J. M. Quijano Otero' (printed p. 297); PDF page 311 is printed p. 299, 'Indicaciones generales / Signos', and the sentence 'Estos son los únicos signos modales. Para la acentuación pinto el acento allí donde lo he oído de viva voz, pues por regla general puede asentarse que el acento carga sobre la última sílaba.' is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the final syllable as a general rule; the author marks the accent orthographically only where he heard it, which implies the rule has exceptions. The 1876 German version of the same manuscript (ZfE 8: 359) gives only 'Accentuation ist der Accent dahin gesetzt, wo ich das Wort habe betonen hören' (the accent is placed where I heard the word stressed) with no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Implied but not listed: the author writes the accent 'where I have heard it', and marked forms in the text include non-final accents (e.g. 'Uárra' boy, 'táma' snake, 'táira' you-pl.), so the 'general rule' is not exceptionless.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms elicited from speakers; 19th-century impressionistic notation by a non-linguist (physician), with no phonetic definition of 'acento'. Low authority; to be superseded by Mortensen 1999 or Loewen 1963 when opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The only opened statement is a 19th-century sketch by the physician José Vicente Uribe (Spanish edition copied and read by J. M. Quijano Otero, 1882; German version 1876). It describes 'embera bede' as spoken across the whole Chocó 'between the mouths of the Atrato and the San Juan and the cordillera bordering Chocó and Antioquia'; the 1876 German version names the Chamí, Andágueda, Murindó, Cañasgordas, Rioverde, Necodá, Caramanta, Tadocito, Pató and Curasamba groups, i.e. Antioquia/upper-Atrato Emberá (Emberá-Chamí [cmi] / Emberá-Catío [cto] = embe1260 territory) as much as Atrato/Darién Emberá. Glottolog files both editions under nort2972 and the 'Darienes' label is the compilers, but the sketch is pan-Emberá rather than tied to modern Northern Emberá [emp] proper. The modern reference grammar (Mortensen 1999) covers Catío [cto] and Northern Emberá [emp] together; Loewen 1958/1963 describe the Sambú (Panama) dialect = emp.

tone_statements.citation: Constenla Umaña, Adolfo & Enrique Margery Peña. 1991. Elementos de fonología comparada chocó. Revista de Filología y Lingüística de la Universidad de Costa Rica 17(1-2): 137-191. doi:10.15517/rfl.v17i1-2.20972.
tone_statements.quote: En general, el tono parece ser más importante que la intensidad (véase, por ejemplo, Rex y Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) en la manifestación fonética del acento y ciertas observaciones de Loewen (1958: 20, nota 4) sugieren incluso la posibilidad de que el sambú sea una lengua tonal, pues al lado de una mayoría de palabras disilábicas que tienen el acento o en la primera sílaba o en la segunda, reconoce la existencia de algunas con igual "acento" en ambas, de las cuales menciona / 'pha'pha/ 'madre', / 'ta'ta/ 'padre', / 'bɯ'tɯ/ 'ardilla'. No obstante, por el momento, todos los autores coinciden en asignar a las lenguas la condición de acentuales
tone_statements.translation: In general, pitch seems to be more important than intensity (see e.g. Rex & Schöttelndreyer 1973: 79) in the phonetic manifestation of the accent, and certain observations by Loewen (1958: 20, note 4) even suggest the possibility that Sambú is a tonal language, since beside a majority of disyllabic words that carry the accent either on the first or on the second syllable, he recognises the existence of some with equal 'accent' on both, of which he mentions /'pha'pha/ 'mother', /'ta'ta/ 'father', /'bɯ'tɯ/ 'squirrel'. Nevertheless, for the time being, all authors agree in assigning the languages the status of accentual (stress) languages [the paragraph continues: in Catío and Sambú the accent may fall on the penult as well as on the final syllable; a free accent is proposed for proto-Emberá].
tone_statements.summary: Stress-accent language by consensus, accent cued mainly by pitch; lexical accent position contrastive (penult or final) in Sambú = Northern Emberá; Loewen's level-'accented' disyllables raise, but do not establish, a tonal analysis; no tone inventory proposed.
